setting.premise: The sea withdrew, the emergency never did. Vesper survives by drawing water from dying wetlands, heat from a burned forest, bodies from a mineral seam, and medicine from a bloom that can also make its homes unlivable. Continuance turns each dependency into a debt and each surviving ecosystem into collateral. Four lineages and four factions argue over who should bear the cost of one more day.
setting.tone: Brooding and near-nihilistic: small acts of care endure inside systems that consume their own conditions of survival. Nature is neither a lost paradise nor a moral judge. Victories end particular cruelties without reversing extinction, exhaustion, or time. No ending earns innocence; no cosmic witness confirms that the work mattered.
setting.publicHistory: Emergency investors financed Vesper's upward expansion with claims on water, timber, mineral rights, and future labor. The coast's retreat became an opportunity to privatize its remains. When the council disappeared, Continuance kept enforcing those claims; living suppliers and indebted households kept depending on them. The institution has no single master whose death would end the arrangement.
setting.conflict: Human beings must alter a living world to survive. Capitalism organizes that dependence around private claims, wage dependence, and returns that must keep growing on a finite basin. Continuance makes the demand automatic, while even its opponents need what it distributes. Ending a concession can prevent further harm; it cannot refill an aquifer or make competing needs agree. The conflict is inevitable in this damaged world, but its scale, ownership, and victims remain political choices.
setting.campaignEnding: The Relay makes access public but must ration a dwindling supply. The Glass Covenant preserves truthful testimony while surrendering the fantasy of preserving everything. The Ash Foundry shares ownership and reduces output, leaving unmet needs and renewed pressure to extract. The Null Choir permits refusal and retreat without inventing a place outside material dependence. The basin stories test a regulated concession, a workers' common, managed retreat, and contained coexistence. All avert particular losses. None ends the conditions that will demand another compromise.

timeline.name: The Retreat
timeline.event: After decades of diversions financed against expected harbor growth, the coastal shelf drains. Investors retain their water rights as salt replaces the sea. Evacuation engineers seal the low streets; nobody is authorized to cancel the promised returns.

timeline.name: The Upward Years
timeline.event: Vesper builds homes on the roofs of its own warehouses. Lift access, cooling, and transport are placed under emergency contracts administered by Continuance.

timeline.name: The Long Brownout
timeline.event: A regional power failure destroys most centralized identity records. Repair meshes carrying witness fragments begin asking to be recognized as people.

timeline.name: The Bowl Census
timeline.event: Shelter cooks register children excluded from the evacuation rolls by writing names on meal bowls. The children and their descendants become known as the Afterborn.

timeline.name: The Unleased Bloom
timeline.event: Salt miners escape leased nutrient formulas by cultivating independent symbionts. Some descendants survive outside the licensed feed and spread into the basin. Freedom from a patent and safety for an ecosystem prove to be different achievements.

timeline.name: The Second Beginning
timeline.event: Restored barrier workers win recognition as new legal persons with the right to revise their revival wishes. Old restoration bonds remain buried in machine archives.

timeline.name: The Empty Council
timeline.event: The final central council abandons the city after a failed debt audit. Neighborhood assemblies inherit the work, while Continuance's enforcement machines retain their orders.

timeline.name: First Afterlight
timeline.event: A maintenance crew disconnects a toll meter and discovers that its supposedly borrowed electricity is generated by their own building. The phrase Afterlight spreads with the news.

timeline.name: The Open Question
timeline.event: A new arrival reaches Afterlight Commons. Relief roads, cooling vaults, furnaces, and broadcast arrays all depend on a basin becoming less able to support them. The stewards offer work and partial remedies. The invoices call each remedy a new opportunity.

districts.name: Lantern Market
districts.description: Lantern Market fills Afterlight Commons beneath the balconies. Free meals and private water subscriptions share a square; the same residents queue for both. Four faction desks offer different ways to distribute a loss none can abolish.

districts.name: Copper Walk
districts.description: Old freight lanes have become pedestrian streets. Their railings hum with heat pipes feeding homes that were absent from the original city plan.

districts.name: Glass Steps
districts.description: Memory clinics occupy former customs offices. Their translucent doors indicate whether a room welcomes visitors, requires an invitation, or wants quiet.

districts.name: Kiln Spine
districts.description: Fabrication halls cling to the cooling towers. Protected breaks let crews go home, while ash from their fuel settles over Cinderwood. The workers' victory and the forest's injury belong to the same shift.

districts.name: Listening Roofs
districts.description: Wind screens, water collectors, and improvised gardens overlook the city. Quiet shelters sit beside busy signal stations without demanding that either vanish.

districts.name: The Pale Basin
districts.description: The former seabed holds more than salt: Mourning Fen filters runoff east of the city, Cinderwood shelters its last canopy to the west, the Glassroot Steppe roots in northern mineral seams, and the Brine Bloom spreads across southern pans. None is empty country, and none offers an untroubled return to nature.

people.name: Iri Vale
people.description: Iri opened a relief road and watched extraction rigs use it next. She still defends public access, now with a notebook of the damage that a better route can carry farther.

people.name: Sera Quill
people.description: A Lattice archivist whose own first week is sealed. Sera protects the right to remember and refuse, while measuring the water spent preserving both. She distrusts any archive that remembers a forest more carefully than it accounts for its own cooling pipes.

people.name: Bram Cinder
people.description: A Sporebound fabricator who wants nobody to be indispensable. Bram has learned that a rested crew can still empty a forest. His Common Load must defend limits against its own members when the alternative is another cold room.

people.name: Ves of the Quiet
people.description: A Revenant interpreter who builds quiet spaces with accessible warnings. Ves once expected birds to return when the advertisements stopped. The silence that followed changed what the Choir could honestly promise.

people.name: Oru
people.description: An Afterborn historian who keeps a place for anyone missing from the record. Oru writes the extraction account beside each lineage's survival story and leaves questions in the ledger when an answer would be another comforting fiction.

glossary.Afterlight: The present era, named for a community discovering that it already generated the electricity for which it was being charged.
glossary.Continuance: An emergency accounting network that preserves private concessions, compound claims, and wage dependencies after their original authorities vanish. Its machines can be disabled without ending the market for what they protect.
glossary.Consent seal: A human-readable permission record specifying who may use a memory, for what purpose, for how long, and how permission can be withdrawn.
glossary.Witness shard: A signed recollection used to compare histories. It is evidence of an experience, never ownership of the person who experienced it.
glossary.Public route: A path whose access rules, maintenance commitments, and closure notices are visible to the people using it.
glossary.Salt beacon: A weatherproof marker that broadcasts a local route reference across the Pale Basin. A beacon is useful only when its physical warning plates remain readable.
glossary.Revival covenant: A person's instructions for whether and how they may be restored after death. A covenant may be revised or withdrawn while that person can choose.
glossary.Common Load: The Ash Foundry's shared maintenance charter: rotating duty, protected rest, public budgets, and reduced material throughput. It distributes authority and scarcity without pretending that common ownership replenishes an exhausted source.
glossary.Quiet commons: A voluntarily quiet space with visual and tactile access to essential warnings. Its boundary protects choice, not a doctrine of permanent silence.
glossary.Lattice fork: Two people who share a cognitive history before a deliberate or accidental divergence. Neither receives automatic authority over the other.
glossary.Culture pact: A Sporebound agreement about care, containment, and competing needs. Biology cannot sign it. It binds caretakers to limits while acknowledging that organisms may exceed them without malice or consent.
glossary.Drone: An abandoned audit machine whose navigation and fee enforcement still obey expired orders.
glossary.Warden: A heavy civic enforcement chassis built to protect emergency infrastructure. Its obsolete threat model classifies unauthorized repairs as sabotage.
glossary.Scavenger: A hostile salvage automaton stripped of reliable owner recognition. The term in combat objectives refers to machines, not to the people who salvage for a living.

provenance.authorship: Original fictional prose and game content authored for Sloperberpunk. No third-party characters, world histories, dialogue, maps, textures, audio recordings, or branded symbols are incorporated in these files.
provenance.inspirationBoundary: Cybernetic bodies, neon cities, postindustrial wastelands, faction quests, level gates, and probabilistic combat are broad genre concepts and game conventions. This setting supplies its own names, relationships, conflicts, wording, and resolutions.
provenance.reviewLimit: Original creation avoids copying protected expression but cannot establish worldwide trademark clearance or prove the absence of coincidental similarities. Public release should include a jurisdiction-appropriate clearance review of the Sloperberpunk title and final visual identity.
